name: Lysimachus
charge: Sacrilege: robbing the temple with Menelaus’ consent
summary: Left as his brother’s deputy, Lysimachus committed many sacrileges in the city by the consent of Menelaus, and much gold was already carried away when the report of it spread. The multitude gathered against him, and he armed about three thousand men and began the violence himself, with an old man named Auranus leading them. The people answered with stones, clubs and handfuls of dust, wounded and scattered the force, and killed the temple robber beside the treasury.
offenseFull: Menelaus, called to account for the money he had promised the king, left his brother Lysimachus in his place as his deputy (2 Maccabees 4:29). The temple was handed to the same house that had already sold it, and the brother of the man who first betrayed the treasury was now guarding the door of it. Many sacrileges were committed in the city by Lysimachus with the consent of Menelaus, and the report of it was spread abroad, many vessels of gold being already carried away (2 Maccabees 4:39). The history class puts it bluntly: this man was robbing the place openly, and the gold was gone before anyone moved.

When the multitude gathered themselves together against him, the common people rose filled with rage, and Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and began first to offer violence, Auranus being the leader of them, a man far gone in years and no less in folly (2 Maccabees 4:40). An old man, the class said, and evil with it; age had taught him nothing. Rather than restore what was taken, the plunderer answered the protest of his own countrymen with an army of three thousand.
judgmentFull: They that saw the attempt of Lysimachus caught up stones, and others clubs, and some took handfuls of dust that was next at hand and cast them all together upon Lysimachus and those that set upon them; many of them they wounded, some they struck to the ground, and all of them they forced to flee. As for the temple robber himself, him they killed beside the treasury (2 Maccabees 4:41-42). The people had no weapons and used what was under their feet. The place he had plundered was the place where his hired force could no longer keep him.

The corruption did not die with him. Of these matters an accusation was laid against Menelaus, and when the king came to Tyre three men sent from the senate pleaded the cause before him; but Menelaus, being convicted, promised Ptolemy the son of Dorymenes much money to pacify the king toward him and was discharged, while they that followed the matter for the city, for the people and for the holy vessels were condemned to death, and they of Tyre, moved with hatred of that wicked deed, buried them honourably (2 Maccabees 4:43-49). So through the covetousness of them that were in power Menelaus remained still in authority (2 Maccabees 4:50). The man who guarded the sacrilege with soldiers fell at the treasury; the man who bought the king kept the office. The history class reads the whole run of it as one covetousness working its way through a single family until every man in it was dead in disgrace.

lawsResolved.text: You shall not steal another's property.
Priests are to keep the charge of the sanctuary and tabernacle of the congregation and keep it supplied and in proper order.
God executes judgment here on the earth.
The congregation of the people (jury) can judge matters in a criminal case.

text.text: Now Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus in his stead in the priesthood; and Sostratus left Crates, who was governor of the Cyprians.

Now when many sacrileges had been committed in the city by Lysimachus with the consent of Menelaus, and the fruit thereof was spread abroad, the multitude gathered themselves together against Lysimachus, many vessels of gold being already carried away.

Whereupon the common people rising, and being filled with rage, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men, and began first to offer violence; one Auranus being the leader, a man far gone in years, and no less in folly.

They then seeing the attempt of Lysimachus, some of them caught stones, some clubs, others taking handfuls of dust, that was next at hand, cast them all together upon Lysimachus, and those that set upon them.
Thus many of them they wounded, and some they struck to the ground, and all of them they forced to flee: but as for the churchrobber himself, him they killed beside the treasury.
Of these matters therefore there was an accusation laid against Menelaus.
Now when the king came to Tyrus, three men that were sent from the senate pleaded the cause before him:
But Menelaus, being now convicted, promised Ptolemee the son of Dorymenes to give him much money, if he would pacify the king toward him.
Whereupon Ptolemee taking the king aside into a certain gallery, as it were to take the air, brought him to be of another mind:

Insomuch that he discharged Menelaus from the accusations, who notwithstanding was cause of all the mischief: and those poor men, who, if they had told their cause, yea, before the Scythians, should have been judged innocent, them he condemned to death.
Thus they that followed the matter for the city, and for the people, and for the holy vessels, did soon suffer unjust punishment.
Wherefore even they of Tyrus, moved with hatred of that wicked deed, caused them to be honourably buried.
And so through the covetousness of them that were of power Menelaus remained still in authority, increasing in malice, and being a great traitor to the citizens.
If a man shall steal an ox, or a sheep, and kill it, or sell it; he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.
The hands of the witnesses shall be first upon him to put him to death, and afterward the hands of all the people. So thou shalt put the evil away from among you.
